situation.note: I have been trying to build apps on the side for years now and none of them have really worked. I keep going but I don't know what I am doing wrong anymore. I have a job, kids, my parents to look after, and this thing I keep failing at.

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call holding on to how it turns out, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the doubt and the weight of years of trying, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that doubt and delay feed each other, and that waiting to feel ready keeps you stuck.
week_beats.steady: You hold that your own path walked imperfectly is enough, and no honest effort is ever wasted.
week_beats.story: A man who kept going through years of failure shows you what it means to act without the result.

understanding.core_struggle: A midlife professional juggling work, children, and aging parents feels they are failing at a side project they have kept trying on for years, and wonders what they are doing wrong.
understanding.mirror: Years of trying and nothing to show for it, while the rest of your life asks for everything else.
understanding.insight: You are tired of the side project, and you are tired of being told you are failing at it. The doubt has settled in because the effort has not yet met the result.
understanding.mechanism_label: Holding on to how it turns out

queries.hook: The weight of years of trying and the doubt that you are failing at the one thing that is yours, while the rest of your life asks for everything else.
queries.diagnose: Doubt and delay feed each other; waiting to feel ready keeps you stuck, and the unacted-on decision weighs more than the work itself.
queries.steady: Your own path walked imperfectly is enough; no honest effort on the right path is ever wasted.
queries.act: Rise and act; do the work fully and let the result go, one day at a time, and keep at it without waiting to feel ready.
queries.story: A man who spent years trying to build something of his own, met repeated failure, and kept going until the work itself became his answer.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse.sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाचअयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः । अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति ॥
verse.line: What happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't make it to the end?
verse.translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection, what end does he come to, Krishna?
verse.why: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

matched.label: I can't tell if continuing is discipline or stubbornness

prasang.title: What becomes of one who falls from yoga
prasang.summary: Arjuna fears that one who falls short is lost like a torn cloud. Krishna promises that no one who does good comes to ruin; past effort carries forward and they strive again.
prasang.lesson: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what happens to someone who starts with faith but slips before reaching the goal. Krishna answers that no sincere effort is ever lost. The work done before the fall remains, and the person simply begins again from the point they left off, without starting from nothing.
verse.for_you: You have been trying to build these apps for years, and the doubt is heavy because the result has not come. But the effort itself is not erased. The code you wrote, the ideas you tested, the time you gave it, all of it stays with you.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing from your past attempts that you can carry forward.
verse.scene_line: You are Arjuna on the field, asking if the fall matters.
asks: What does it mean to start again from where I left off?
How do I know if my past effort still counts?
What if the fall was bigger than I thought?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on action: a riddle of questions and answers.
verse.sanskrit: को लाभो गुणिसङ्गमः किमसुखं प्राज्ञेतरैः सङ्गतिः का हानिः समयच्युतिर्निपुणता का धर्मतत्त्वे रतिः । कः शूरो विजितेन्द्रियः प्रियतमा कानुव्रता किं धनं विद्या किं सुखमप्रवासगमनं राज्यं किमाज्ञाफलम् ॥
verse.line: What is real loss? Missing your moment. Who is a hero? One who has mastered himself.
verse.translation: What is gain? The company of the virtuous. What is sorrow? The company of fools. What is loss? Missing the right moment. What is skill? Love for the heart of dharma. Who is a hero? One who has mastered the senses. Who is a beloved? A faithful wife. What is wealth? Learning. What is happiness? Not having to live abroad. What is a kingdom? Having one's word obeyed.
verse.why: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.
verse.misuse: 'Happiness is not living abroad' voices homesickness; it is not a verdict on emigrants.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari, a king who stepped down from his throne, asks the reader a series of riddles about what truly matters. He asks what real loss is, and answers it is missing your moment. He asks who is a hero, and answers it is one who has mastered themselves. He shows that your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to. The verse proposes that your worth is measured by how you manage yourself, not by the rewards you receive or the moment you fear losing.
verse.for_you: You have spent years building these apps. The delay and the doubt are feeding each other, and waiting to feel ready keeps you stuck. The effort has not met the result yet, and that is where the doubt lives. Your actions are the one thing that matters, not the result.
verse.try_today: Notice when you are waiting to feel ready before you begin.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own waiting room, and the moment is passing.
asks: How do I master myself when the app fails?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
verse.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
verse.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to anyone who has ever been judged by the world while doing what they believe is right. The scene is one of quiet resolve. People are talking. Money is uncertain. Death is a shadow in the background. The verse says that the steady person does not leave the path of what is right, no matter what happens around them.
verse.for_you: You have spent years building apps. The results are not there. People around you may judge that. But your path is the steady work itself. You do not need the outcome to be right. You could stay on the path of trying. Your part is the honest effort.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment of your effort today and call it enough.
verse.scene_line: You are standing at the edge of the ocean, and the churning has not yet shown nectar.
asks: How do I know if I am steady or just stuck?
What if the path I am on is not the right one?
How do I measure my part when the result is missing?

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
verse.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
verse.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
verse.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu, a teacher of the highest kind, speaks to Nidagha, his student, who is living an ordinary life in a village. The student asks how a person can be free while still doing ordinary work. Ribhu tells him to keep walking his path, but to let go of how it ends. Do the work at hand, take what comes, speak gently, and treat the world as family. Move through the world with a clear mind. Act fully, but do not let the doing agitate you inside.
verse.for_you: The apps you build are the work at hand, and the doubt is the agitation. You do not have to prove the project works today to prove your effort was real. Your path walked imperfectly is enough. No honest effort is ever wasted.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today where you let go of the result and just do the work.
verse.scene_line: You are the student walking the village path, and the teacher says to keep walking.
asks: How do I know when to stop trying?
Can I let go of the result and still care?

verse.speaker: Angada
verse.setting: The monkeys searching for Sita are exhausted and failing; young Angada rallies them.
verse.sanskrit: अवश्यं कुर्वतां तस्य दृश्यते कर्मणः फलम्। परं निर्वेदमागम्य नहि नोन्मीलनं क्षमम्॥
verse.line: Keep working and the results will come. Sink into despair and it is hard to get back up.
verse.translation: Those who keep working surely see the fruit of their work. But once you sink into deep despair, you cannot rise again.
verse.why: Missing a deadline feels final; it rarely is.

prasang.title: The missed deadline
prasang.summary: The southern search party loses time in a magic cave and misses Sugriva's deadline. Angada rallies them once, then despairs, fearing punishment and certain he will be blamed. Hanuman reasons with him to return.
prasang.story_hook: They came out of the cave to find that spring had already come, and their deadline had gone.
prasang.lesson: Missing a deadline feels final; it rarely is.

verse.meaning: Young Angada leads the monkey search party. They have lost time in a magic cave and missed Sugriva's deadline. Angada despairs, fearing blame, and tells the group to give up. Hanuman reasons with him, saying that sinking into despair makes it harder to rise than working on. Angada agrees to continue. The verse says those who keep working will see fruit. Once you sink into deep despair, you cannot rise again.
verse.for_you: The years of trying and the quiet failure have pushed you toward a place where stopping feels like the only honest choice. Angada saw his own search party give up, and he knew that despair is a trap that makes rising impossible.
verse.try_today: Write down one small task for the project and do it.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the edge of a cave, the deadline missed, and despair waits to swallow the path.
asks: How do I separate the missed deadline from the whole project?
What if the despair is just a heavy blanket I can lift?
Where is the next small step I can take without looking ahead?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse.sanskrit: कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन । मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
verse.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

words.en: cause of the fruit of action

verse.why: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.
verse.misuse: This is not 'don't care about results' or 'don't plan'. Care, plan and aim well; just don't let the outcome own you.

prasang.title: The yoga of action
prasang.summary: Krishna teaches the yoga of action: work wholeheartedly, give up clinging to outcomes, stay even in success and failure, and keep a single steady purpose.
prasang.lesson: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

verse.meaning: Krishna stands with Arjuna on the field, seeing him paralyzed by the weight of what will happen if he fights. The stakes are life and death, and Arjuna is frozen because he is clinging to the outcome. Krishna tells him to act, to do the work fully, and to release the burden of controlling the results. The point is not to stop caring, but to stop letting the result own the mind.
verse.for_you: The apps you build are the work. The downloads, the praise, the money, the failure, all of it is the fruit. You are trying to own the fruit before it is even on the tree.
verse.try_today: Do one small part of the work, then close the laptop and leave it.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the edge of the field, holding your bow, waiting for a future you cannot see.
asks: How do I do the work and still let it go?
Can I keep going if I no longer hold the result?

story.title: Bali tires of endless days and asks his father's riddle
story.story_hook: Bali had conquered everything there was to conquer, and one evening he realised he was bored.
story.summary: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day at his window he realises he is doing the same things day after day, night after night, and asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him: a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind; win it over, by practice, and everything is won.
story.lesson: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

anchor.speaker: Virochana
anchor.setting: Bali's father Virochana tells him the secret of mastering the mind.
anchor.sanskrit: एषा ह्यत्यन्तदुष्प्रापा सुप्रापा च महामते । अनभ्यस्तातिदुष्प्रापा स्वभ्यस्ता प्राप्यते सुखम् ॥
anchor.line: Unpractised, it feels impossible. Well practised, it comes easily.
anchor.translation: This is extremely hard to attain and also easy, great-minded one: unpractised, it is very hard to reach; well practised, it comes easily.
anchor.why: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

prasang.title: Bali tires of endless days and asks his father's riddle
prasang.summary: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day at his window he realises he is doing the same things day after day, night after night, and asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him: a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind; win it over, by practice, and everything is won.
prasang.story_hook: Bali had conquered everything there was to conquer, and one evening he realised he was bored.
prasang.lesson: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

story.hook_title: A demon king who had conquered everything realised one evening that he was bored
story.teaser: A demon king who had conquered everything realised one evening that he was bored
story.for_you: Bali ruled the worlds and still felt the same loop. You have built apps for years, and the loop is the same: the code, the hope, the quiet letdown. The question is not whether the next app will make it.
asks: What does my mind need to feel steady today?
How do I tell the difference between discipline and stubbornness?
